questions.text:
Which of the following languages is generated by the given grammar?
[latex]S\rightarrow aS|bS|\varepsilon[/latex]
questions.solution:
[latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid bS\mid\varepsilon[/latex] adds any a or b at each step, in any order and any number of times, so it generates every string over {a, b}, including [latex]\varepsilon[/latex].

Answer: {a,b}*

questions.text: Let [latex]R_{1}[/latex] and [latex]R_{2}[/latex] be regular sets defined over the alphabet, then
questions.solution:
Regular languages are closed under union, intersection, star and complement.

[latex]\Sigma^*-R_1[/latex] is the complement of [latex]R_1[/latex], so it is regular.

Answer: [latex]\Sigma^*-R_1[/latex] is regular

questions.text:
Which of the following languages are context-free?
[latex]L_{1}=\{a^{m}b^{n}a^{n}b^{m}|m,n\geq 1\}[/latex]
[latex]L_{2}=\{a^{m}b^{n}a^{m}b^{n}|m,n\geq 1\}[/latex]
[latex]L_{3}=\{a^{m}b^{n}|m=2n+1\}[/latex]
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]L_1=a^mb^na^nb^m[/latex]: nested matching (outer m, inner n) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] push a's, push b's, pop on a's, pop on b's [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL.
- [latex]L_2=a^mb^na^mb^n[/latex]: crossed matching, which one stack cannot do [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not CFL.
- [latex]L_3=a^{2n+1}b^n[/latex]: push for a's, pop for b's [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL.

Answer: L1 and L3 only

questions.text: Let L be the language represented by the regular expression [latex]\Sigma ^{*}0011\Sigma ^{*}[/latex] where [latex]\Sigma[/latex]={0,1}. What is the minimum number of states in a DFA that recognizes [latex]\bar{L}[/latex] (complement of L)?
questions.solution:
A DFA for "contains 0011" tracks progress: nothing, 0, 00, 001, 0011 (trap accepting) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 states.

The complement uses the same DFA with final and non-final states swapped, so it also needs 5 states.

Answer: 5

questions.text:
Consider the alphabet [latex]\Sigma[/latex]={0, 1}, the null/empty string [latex]\lambda[/latex] and the sets of strings [latex]X_{0}, X_{1}, \; and \; X_{2}[/latex] generated by the corresponding non-terminals of a regular grammar. [latex]X_{0}, X_{1}, \; and \; X_{2}[/latex] are related as follows.
[latex]X_{0}=1X_{1}[/latex]
[latex]X_{1},=0X_{1}+1 X_{2}[/latex]
[latex]X_{2}=0X_{1}+ \{\lambda\}[/latex]
Which one of the following choices precisely represents the strings in [latex]X_{0}[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Substitute [latex]X_2[/latex] into [latex]X_1[/latex]:
[latex]X_1=0X_1+1(0X_1+\lambda)=(0+10)X_1+1[/latex]

By Arden's rule [latex]X_1=(0+10)^*1[/latex], so [latex]X_0=1(0+10)^*1[/latex].

Answer: 1(0 + 10)*1
